subChunks.title: Tracing Enslaved and Freed Ancestors in the Caribbean and Atlantic World
subChunks.hookHtml: The genealogy of the African diaspora in the Caribbean and the Atlantic world is among the most challenging and most urgent work in the field. The transatlantic slave trade transported approximately 12.5 million people from West and Central Africa to the Americas between 1500 and 1870; for the descendants of those who were enslaved, reconstructing family history requires navigating records created within, and often deliberately designed to obscure, the institution of slavery. Yet records do exist — the British colonial administration in particular generated detailed registers of enslaved people in the years before emancipation, and the records of colonial planters, churches, and government are increasingly digitised and accessible.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Slave Registers (1813–1834) — the most important pre-emancipation source

Following the abolition of the British slave trade in 1807, the British Parliament required colonial governments to maintain triennial registers of all enslaved people in British Caribbean colonies. These registers — covering Jamaica, Barbados, Trinidad, St Kitts, Nevis, Antigua, Dominica, St Lucia, Grenada, and other colonies — are extraordinary genealogical documents:

  • Each register gives the enslaved person's name, age (or birth year), sex, colour (a legally defined category reflecting degree of African ancestry, including 'black,' 'mulatto,' and 'sambo'), occupation, and the name of the enslaver.
  • Comparative registers (comparing one triennial return to the next) record births, deaths, and changes in status.
  • The registers effectively name individuals who are otherwise invisible in colonial records — the first time, for many, that names appear in an official document.
  • The Slave Registers are held at TNA in the T71 series and are fully digitised on Ancestry (free with a card from many UK libraries).

Compensation records — Legacies of British Slave-ownership

When slavery was abolished in the British Empire (1833, effective 1834), the British government paid £20 million in compensation — not to the enslaved people, but to the enslavers. The Slave Compensation Commission created detailed records for every compensated enslaver:

  • Schedules listing the enslaved people attached to each claim, with their names and sometimes ages
  • The Legacies of British Slave-ownership database (ucl.ac.uk/lbs) at University College London has digitised the compensation records and linked them to biographical information on slave-owners — an extraordinary research tool for identifying enslaver families and their connections.

Manumission records and free coloured registers

Enslaved people who were freed before emancipation (by purchase, by their enslaver's will, or by manumission) appear in:

  • Manumission registers: notarial records of formal freedom grants; held in colonial archives in the relevant islands.
  • Free coloured registers: in some colonies, free people of African descent were required to register; these registers are at colonial or national archives.

Church records in the Caribbean

Anglican, Catholic, and Moravian churches in the Caribbean baptised enslaved people in varying degrees:

  • Anglican parish registers for Caribbean colonies are at TNA (CO5 and CO series) and at the relevant island's national archive; some on FindMyPast and FamilySearch.
  • The Moravian Church baptised enslaved people extensively in the Lesser Antilles (Antigua, St Kitts, Jamaica) from the 18th century and kept meticulous registers with individual names — sometimes more detailed than Anglican registers.
  • Catholic records are particularly important for Trinidad, St Lucia, Martinique, and Guadeloupe (French colonies).

The slave voyage database and African origins

For tracing ancestry before arrival in the Caribbean — back to Africa — the tools are:

  • Slave Voyages database (slavevoyages.org): documents approximately 36,000 transatlantic slave voyages, giving the departure port in Africa (regional or specific), the number of enslaved people, and the arrival port in the Americas. It cannot name individuals but establishes likely regions of African origin for specific voyages.
  • African Names Database: a subset of Slave Voyages that names approximately 91,000 individuals recorded in the liberated African registers of Sierra Leone (1808–1864) — Africans intercepted from illegal slave ships after 1807 and recorded by British authorities. Gives name, age, ethnicity, and embarkation region. A named ancestor can be identified if they were intercepted.
  • DNA testing: African ancestry reference populations on AncestryDNA and 23andMe give broad regional origin estimates (e.g., Yoruba in Nigeria, Igbo in Nigeria, Akan in Ghana). These are population-level estimates, not specific community identifications, but can narrow the geographic search area.

Post-emancipation records

After emancipation (1834–1838 in British colonies; 1865 in the US; 1888 in Brazil), formerly enslaved people began to appear in civil registration systems:

  • British Caribbean civil registration began at different dates per colony: Jamaica 1878, Barbados 1891, Trinidad 1848.
  • The 1844 Trinidad census is an extraordinary document: taken six years after emancipation, it lists formerly enslaved people by name, age, place of origin (African nation or island), occupation, and location — one of the only early post-emancipation censuses in the Caribbean to name individuals.
  • Caribbean genealogical records are increasingly at national archives (Jamaica Archives, Barbados Archives, etc.) with some on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

storyBeats.text: Theodora opens the TNA T71 Slave Register on a screen — a printed ledger with columns for name, colour, age, sex, occupation. Each row a person. Hundreds of rows on each page.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: The Slave Registers are a paradox: records of profound human injustice that are simultaneously among the richest genealogical sources for Caribbean ancestry. The British colonial government required these registers from 1813 because it needed to prevent illegal slave importation after the trade was banned in 1807. The result — unintentionally, from the perspective of genealogy — is that every enslaved person in a British Caribbean colony was named in an official document for the first time. Name. Age. Occupation. The enslaver's name. This is the record that makes reconstruction possible.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: And the Legacies of British Slave-ownership database — the compensation records for the enslaver families. Twenty million pounds paid to slave-owners in 1834. Every payment recorded. Every name of every enslaver, the number of enslaved people they claimed compensation for, and their identities. This database maps the financial infrastructure of slavery — and for genealogists it maps which families owned whom. If you know the enslaver's name from the Slave Register, the LBS database gives you the full compensation picture.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Anchor Caribbean and Atlantic slavery records

Retrieve from memory:

  • What are the Slave Registers (T71) and what information do they record?
  • What is the Legacies of British Slave-ownership database and what does it document?
  • What is the Slave Voyages database and what can it tell a genealogist?
  • Why are Moravian Church records particularly valuable for Caribbean genealogy?
  • What is the genealogical significance of the 1844 Trinidad census?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
The Slave Registers (T71 at TNA) are triennial registers of enslaved people in British Caribbean colonies from 1813 to 1834, required by Parliament to prevent illegal slave importation after the 1807 abolition of the trade. They record each enslaved person's name, age, sex, colour (a legal category), occupation, and the enslaver's name — often the first time an enslaved individual was named in an official document. Fully digitised on Ancestry.

The Legacies of British Slave-ownership (LBS) database (ucl.ac.uk/lbs) at University College London documents the compensation paid to British enslavers after the Slavery Abolition Act 1833. It names enslavers, gives the number of enslaved people per claim, and links to biographical information about the enslaver families — useful for identifying which enslaver families were connected and tracing the paper trail of slavery's financial history.

The Slave Voyages database (slavevoyages.org) documents approximately 36,000 transatlantic slave voyages, giving departure region in Africa, number of enslaved people, and arrival port in the Americas. It cannot name individuals but helps establish likely African regions of origin for specific voyages and routes.

Moravian Church records are valuable for Caribbean genealogy because the Moravian mission extensively baptised enslaved people in the Lesser Antilles from the 18th century onward, keeping meticulous registers with individual names — sometimes more complete than Anglican registers for enslaved populations.

The 1844 Trinidad census is significant because, taken six years after emancipation, it lists formerly enslaved people by name, age, African nation or island of origin, occupation, and location — one of the only early post-emancipation Caribbean censuses to name individuals and give African origins.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Using Caribbean slavery records — a research problem

Your ancestor Samuel Clarke appears in the 1881 Jamaican census in the parish of St Elizabeth, age 47, farmer. Family oral history says his parents were enslaved on the Chambers plantation in St Elizabeth. You want to establish Samuel's parents. Design a research strategy (300–400 words) using the record types covered in this chunk.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Step 1 — Slave Registers (T71): Search TNA T71 Slave Registers for Jamaica, parish of St Elizabeth, for the Chambers plantation. The registers (1813–1834) will list enslaved people on the Chambers estate by name and age. To find Samuel's parents, who would have been enslaved c.1820–1834, identify adult enslaved people of appropriate age (father born c.1790–1810; mother born c.1800–1820). The comparative registers (between successive triennial entries) will show births — if Samuel was born on the plantation c.1834, his birth may appear as an addition to the register.

Step 2 — Compensation records (LBS database): Search the Legacies of British Slave-ownership database for 'Chambers' in St Elizabeth, Jamaica. The compensation claim will confirm the number of enslaved people and may give their names or reference a schedule. This also identifies the Chambers family, enabling further research into estate papers.

Step 3 — Jamaican Anglican baptism registers: The Anglican parish of St Elizabeth held baptismal registers. Search for Samuel Clarke's baptism c.1833–1835. If he was baptised, the register may give his mother's name. Moravian mission records in Jamaica are also worth checking.

Step 4 — Post-emancipation records: Emancipation in Jamaica was in 1834 (with an apprenticeship period to 1838). The Jamaican apprenticeship registers (1834–1838) continued to list formerly enslaved people by estate and name. Search for Clarke family members in the St Elizabeth apprenticeship records.

Step 5 — Freedmen's records and civil registration: Jamaica introduced civil registration in 1878. Search for Samuel Clarke's marriage and death records; his death certificate (if post-1878) may name his parents, giving the mother's maiden name or the father's name.

Step 6 — DNA testing: Test living Clarke descendants for West African ethnicity estimates. Shared DNA matches with other St Elizabeth Caribbean descendants may cluster by plantation of origin through genealogical network analysis.

A UCL database (ucl.ac.uk/lbs) documenting the £20 million paid in compensation to British enslavers after the 1833 Abolition Act — naming enslavers, their enslaved people counts, and biographical information; essential for identifying enslaver families.

A free database (slavevoyages.org) documenting approximately 36,000 transatlantic slave voyages with departure region in Africa, enslaved people count, and arrival port — establishing likely African regional origins for Caribbean ancestors.

A Slave Voyages subset naming approximately 91,000 Africans intercepted from illegal slave ships (1808–1864) and recorded in Sierra Leone liberated African registers — giving name, age, ethnicity, and embarkation region.

A formal legal document granting freedom to an enslaved person before emancipation — recorded in colonial notarial registers and held in Caribbean national archives; among the few pre-emancipation records naming a free individual.

questions.questionHtml: What are the Slave Registers (T71 at TNA) and why were they created?
options: Triennial registers of all enslaved people in British Caribbean colonies (1813–1834), required by Parliament to prevent illegal slave importation after the 1807 abolition of the slave trade — each entry gives the enslaved person's name, age, sex, colour, occupation, and the enslaver's name
Annual lists of slave ships entering British Caribbean ports, compiled by the Royal Navy to enforce the 1807 abolition
Records of compensation paid to enslaved people after emancipation in 1834, listing recipients and amounts
Colonial church baptism registers for enslaved people, required by the Church of England from 1813
questions.correctAnswer: Triennial registers of all enslaved people in British Caribbean colonies (1813–1834), required by Parliament to prevent illegal slave importation after the 1807 abolition of the slave trade — each entry gives the enslaved person's name, age, sex, colour, occupation, and the enslaver's name
questions.explanationHtml: The Slave Registers were established by an 1812 Order in Council and required colonial governments to compile and update registers of all enslaved people every three years. The political motivation was preventing the illegal importation of enslaved people after the British slave trade was abolished in 1807 — by establishing a baseline count, any increase beyond natural population growth would indicate illegal importation. The genealogical consequence is that for the first time, every enslaved person in a British Caribbean colony was named in an official document. The T71 series at TNA covers Jamaica, Barbados, Trinidad, and other colonies; fully digitised on Ancestry.

questions.questionHtml: You find your Jamaican ancestor Mary Brown in the 1817 Slave Register, enslaved on the Hamilton estate, St James Parish, age 25. The 1820 comparative register shows 'Mary Brown — died.' You want to find if Mary had children. What is your next step?
options: Search the 1817 and 1820 registers for children listed under Mary Brown's name or born on the Hamilton estate between 1813 and 1820 — the comparative registers record births as additions; any child born to Mary in this period should appear as an addition with Mary as mother
Search the 1841 Jamaican census for Mary Brown's children — they will all be listed under their mother's name
Mary Brown's death in 1820 means no further records exist for her children
Search the Legacies of British Slave-ownership database for Mary Brown — it lists all enslaved people's children
questions.correctAnswer: Search the 1817 and 1820 registers for children listed under Mary Brown's name or born on the Hamilton estate between 1813 and 1820 — the comparative registers record births as additions; any child born to Mary in this period should appear as an addition with Mary as mother
questions.explanationHtml: The triennial Slave Registers include comparative schedules showing changes between registrations — including births, deaths, purchases, and manumissions. A child born to Mary Brown between the 1813 and 1817 registers would appear as a birth addition in the 1817 register, listed with Mary as the mother. Similarly, any child born between 1817 and 1820 would appear in the 1820 comparative register. The Hamilton estate entries from 1813 to 1820 should be searched in full for children attributed to Mary. After Mary's death in 1820, any surviving children would continue to be listed on the estate register through subsequent triennial returns until emancipation in 1834.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher's DNA test shows 45% 'Nigerian (Yoruba)' ancestry. They conclude their enslaved Caribbean ancestors came from Yorubaland in Nigeria. Is this conclusion sound?
options: Not necessarily — DNA ethnicity estimates are population-level approximations with significant uncertainty; 'Yoruba' as a reference population on testing platforms includes DNA patterns from a broad region that may overlap with neighbouring populations; the result suggests West African origin in the general Yorubaland region but cannot pinpoint a specific community or confirm that enslaved ancestors came from that specific ethnic group
Yes — a 45% result is statistically significant and definitively identifies the ancestral ethnic group
No — DNA tests cannot detect African ancestry at all for people of Caribbean descent
Yes — Yoruba is a highly specific population on all major testing platforms, making this identification precise
questions.correctAnswer: Not necessarily — DNA ethnicity estimates are population-level approximations with significant uncertainty; 'Yoruba' as a reference population on testing platforms includes DNA patterns from a broad region that may overlap with neighbouring populations; the result suggests West African origin in the general Yorubaland region but cannot pinpoint a specific community or confirm that enslaved ancestors came from that specific ethnic group
questions.explanationHtml: DNA ethnicity estimates work by comparing a tested person's DNA segments against reference populations composed of people with documented ancestry from specific regions. The 'Yoruba' reference population on major platforms includes people with ancestry from southwestern Nigeria, but DNA segments don't have clear ethnic labels — the algorithm assigns probability based on similarity to reference populations. A 45% Yoruba result indicates significant West African ancestry in that broad region, but: (1) the reference population itself is based on modern Yoruba-speaking communities, which may not precisely represent the 18th-century population from which enslaved people were taken; (2) neighbouring populations in West Africa share overlapping genetic patterns; (3) the estimate has a margin of error. The result is a useful research lead suggesting a search of the Slave Voyages database for voyages departing from what is now southwestern Nigeria, and might guide DNA match research — but it is not a definitive ethnic identification.
